$comment: S5 judge rubric ROUND 2 (methodology/05-eval-rubric.md #judge) — all 81 items scored fresh on all six dimensions, distractors argued FOR before scoring, by an examiner who did not see round-1 scores until this pass was complete. 0 bounces: no dimension scores ≤2 anywhere. Both round-1 overlap bounces are discharged (d3-q34, d6-q65 — see overlap-report.md and the per-item cases). Round 1 preserved at judge-scores-r1.json.

items.case: Argued FOR: B — a template the whole team vouches for carries real evidence of working output; C — register is what a client first reacts to, so polish is a proxy for acceptance; D — detail is genuinely correlated with prompt quality. All three lose to A on the concept's own terms: each names a proxy (endorsement, register, length) where A names the measure (fitness for the business purpose). Dim2 4: D's 'accepted best practice' is a bare slogan a prepared candidate drops without reading the scenario. Dim3 4: the item tests the judgment standard itself rather than a discriminating application of it. Dim5 3: all three distractors are surface-eliminable archetypes (D12/E02/D14), so the item is right-vs-wrong for a prepared candidate. INTEGRITY: this item's key was visible to the examiner before the blind solve (see blind-solve.json) — Gate 2 should treat its blind result as unverified.

Argued FOR: B — a more senior role does change register and executives do write shorter; D — hand-conversion guarantees the table; E — self-review does catch length overruns sometimes. Each loses: the two observed failures map exactly onto the two absent components, and B/D/E leave the specification incomplete for the next draft. Dim5 3: the stem names the two failures in the same vocabulary as the two keys ('two-page limit', 'benefits table'), so the mapping is mechanical rather than diagnostic.

Argued FOR: A — capability really does lift generic drafts sometimes; C — hand-editing reliably produces distinctive copy; D — some work genuinely is not delegable. All lose: the stem states the officer holds context the request never carried, which is a context gap by definition. Dim5 3: the stem lists the missing elements verbatim and says 'none of which appear in the request', which hands the answer to the reader; the echo screen flagged this item (key-echo 5 vs 3).

Argued FOR: B — richer instructions do improve single-prompt output; C — a multi-agent pipeline genuinely would isolate stages; D — fluent memos are often right. B loses because length is not traceability, C because it buys traceability with machinery a monthly job cannot repay and sits past Associate scope, D because the officer already knows some memos are wrong. Dim3 4: the same decomposition-for-diagnosability discrimination is carried by d1-q06 under a neighbouring concept — see the twin-pair note in the eval report.

Argued FOR: A — client optics are a real project pressure and early deliverables buy goodwill; B — briefings are sometimes clearer written last; D — a single pass keeps the study coherent. All lose to dependency order: every later step inherits the questionnaire's errors. Good-vs-best; the client-pressure surface points away from the principle.

Argued FOR: A — downstream correction does keep output usable; B — tighter wording reduces latitude and often reduces error; C — periodic rewrites are a real hygiene habit. A and B leave the three functions fused and the failure unattributable; C asserts a decay mechanism prompts do not have. Dim2 4: C's invented mechanism is discardable without engaging the scenario. Dim3 4: near-twin of d1-q04.

Argued FOR: B — changing several components at once is faster and the draft has several weak points; C — a proven prompt from another team is real evidence; D — hand-writing is the reliable fallback. B is the confounded-change error the stem's history already demonstrates, C discards the diagnostic in hand, D treats one over-long draft as a ceiling. E01 makes B a genuine near-miss, so the item stays good-vs-best.

Argued FOR: A — more explicit wording sometimes does unlock a stuck prompt; C — a stronger tier is a standard escalation; D — five failed rounds is real evidence of non-delegability. All lose: no wording or tier can cite data never supplied. Dim5 3: the stem states 'no sales data has ever been attached', which is the diagnosis itself; the echo screen flagged the highest key-echo in the bank here (7 vs 2).

Argued FOR: A — more precise definitions is the standard first move and often works; B — self-triage by owners is used in real clinics; D — a daily human re-sort is a safe backstop. A loses because the definitions are already adequate on clear cases, B pushes the judgment onto the least-qualified party, D leaves tomorrow's messages misrouted. A is a strong near-miss, keeping the item good-vs-best.

Argued FOR: A — tight specification is genuinely best practice for most professional work; B — reusing a prompt behind an admired campaign is evidence-based; C — dropping constraints would certainly widen the ideas. A and C both apply one latitude setting to two opposite task types; B is an anecdote about a different brief. The control/range trade-off settles it.

Argued FOR: A — an authoritative briefing is often accurate; C — models are updated, so assuming refresh is not absurd to a lay user; D — a quarterly check is a real control. A mistakes register for currency, C asserts a refresh mechanism that does not exist, D audits after circulation. Dim2 4: C's invented mechanism is eliminable without engaging the scenario.

Argued FOR: B — triaging effort by stakes is exactly what experienced reviewers do; C — time-boxing which reference to check is honest resource management; D — sampling is a legitimate QA design. All three drop a reference the discipline says always runs; only depth flexes. C is the sharp near-miss because it sounds like the same stakes-calibration the key endorses.

Argued FOR: A — every claim was verified, which is the textbook definition of a checked document; C — asking the drafter what it omitted is cheap and sometimes productive; D — client questions do surface gaps. A is the strong tempter and the reason the item works: accuracy checks are structurally blind to omission. Dim5 5: the surface (a thorough, successful fact-check) points away from the principle.

Argued FOR: A — disclosure notices are real practice and do inform readers; B — withdrawing the tool genuinely removes the exposure; D — legal sign-off is a real control for coverage statements. None moves ownership of a shipped claim off the signer. Dim4 4: the rationale's closing appeal to 'why output evaluation carries the largest weight in this credential' argues from exam structure rather than from practitioner vocabulary a candidate can find in study material.

Argued FOR: A — a high self-reported confidence is at least a signal; B — a second pass does catch some errors; C — hedging is standard defensive drafting. All lose to validating a checkable specific against its source. Dim5 3: the stem foregrounds 'the model, asked directly, rates its own confidence as high', which marks the trap rather than concealing it, and the echo screen flagged the key's restatement of the two named specifics.

Argued FOR: A — polish plus specificity plus stated confidence is a lot of converging signal; C — a self-flagging pass narrows what a human must check; D — assuming uncertainty is surfaced is a reasonable lay expectation. All three substitute the model's self-report for an external source. Dim2 4: D asserts an auto-flagging guarantee that does not exist and is discardable on sight. Dim5 3: all three distractors are surface archetypes (E02/D20/D19).

Argued FOR: B — platform safeguards do exist and do block a lot; C — a quarterly audit is a genuine fairness control; D — community feedback is the most authentic signal of harm. B invents a guarantee the drafts have already defeated, C and D are both lagging against a pattern that is publishing weekly. The key's move — widen the routine review's criteria — is the only leading control.

Argued FOR: A — instructing currency is what many practitioners actually type; B — official-sounding register does correlate with official sources; C — waiting for a fresher model is patient and cautious. None creates knowledge the model does not hold; only supplying or retrieving the current rulings does. A is a strong near-miss because it feels like a prompt fix.

Argued FOR: A — thoroughness instructions are ubiquitous and harmless; C — a post-draft fact-check against the pack is a genuinely strong control, arguably stronger than either key; E — confidence scores do sort claims for review. C is the real contender and loses only on the stem's stated constraint: the specialist asked for protection built in at request time, and C is reconstruction at review time. Dim5 5: a defensible option is excluded by a stated constraint rather than by being wrong — the item's difficulty is honest.

Argued FOR: A — cross-run agreement is a real consistency check; B — more copies of the export could plausibly improve reading; D — quarterly hand-verification does catch bad figures. A measures agreement not correctness, B adds volume not arithmetic, D is a detective control for a number that could have been computed. Generated-vs-computed settles it.

Argued FOR: A — reviewers do use fluency as a triage signal in practice; B — tier capability is a real difference; D — deadline pressure is the factor that actually decides review in most teams. Each is a real behaviour and each is exactly what an advance rule exists to overrule. The MR format (2 of 5) keeps the discrimination live.

Argued FOR: B — an intern's sign-off is literally a human in the loop and satisfies a naive reading of the policy; C — disclosure is a real and cheap control; D — the drafter checking its own receipt language would catch arithmetic. B is the strong tempter — it is the compliance-theatre reading of 'mandatory review' — and it loses on qualification plus evidence access. Dim5 5: the surface (a human is already reviewing) points away from the principle.

Argued FOR: A — the source was verified and adaptation is presented as a formatting task, which is the intuitive read; B — re-running the full evaluation is the conservative maximum; D — asking the adapter to confirm fidelity is cheap. A is the trap the item is built on: verification attaches to claims, not documents, and the statistic's strength changed. B over-spends review on claims that did not change. Dim5 5.

Argued FOR: A — fluency is a real proxy for how a retailer will receive a one-pager; C — team preference aggregates judgment; D — matching a competitor's register is a live commercial instinct. All three decide by proxy; only a criterion stated before reading makes the comparison a comparison.

Argued FOR: A — closer proofreading does reduce transcription error; B — redundant statement of dimensions is a real belt-and-braces practice; C — bolding genuinely aids re-keying accuracy. All three preserve the manual transcription step where the errors originate. Dim5 3: the three distractors are all 'keep the prose' variants, so the only structural option is identifiable without engaging the format principle.

Argued FOR: A — five of five is a real result and small teams do ship on less; B — more samples is the standard way to strengthen an evaluation; D — complaint-driven iteration is how most rollouts actually run. B is the sharp near-miss: it adds volume from the same clean distribution and inherits every blind spot. Representativeness, not sample size, is the property at issue.

Argued FOR: B — a user who expects determinism has a coherent model of software and files a reasonable ticket; C — output that varies between runs really is hard to govern; D — template alignment does produce consistent letters. B asserts a determinism never promised, C discards the capability, D treats each symptom downstream. Structural review plus a measured bound is the only response that engages the two grains of variation.

Argued FOR: A — 96% beats the target the team itself set, which is the honest reading of an agreed metric; C — asking crew to confirm safety contacts adds a second check; D — fixing the one sheet is proportionate and fast. A is the designed trap and loses because a severity-class error is not tradable against an average; C pushes the failure onto the protected party; D leaves the mechanism unexamined. Dim6 4: a call-sheet accuracy target expressed as a percentage is slightly constructed for the setting, though not implausible.

Argued FOR: A — a paste snippet genuinely speeds the session up; B — more context does reduce inconsistency; C — a peer firm's working practice is real evidence. A and B optimise the workaround, C is an anecdote about different tasks. Selecting the entry point from the task's shape is the only move that addresses recurrence.

Argued FOR: B — from a lay view every surface reaches the same model; C — a Project is genuinely the right home for recurring comparison work; D — built-in knowledge does cover many institutions. C is the strongest: it is right for a recurring task and wrong only because this one is a one-off. Dim2 4: B's interchangeability claim is flatly false and eliminable on sight.

Argued FOR: A — automation is the obvious efficiency play and the database connection is real; B — handing it to IT puts it with people who build systems; D — visibility with the sponsor board has genuine organisational value. All lose on frequency and stakes: twice a quarter with a manager's review is exactly the interactive-surface profile, and an agent pipeline is past Associate scope besides.

Argued FOR: B — Memory does carry practice forward month to month, which sounds like procedural consistency; C — two runs agreeing is a real arithmetic check people use; E — meticulousness instructions do change output. B is the sharp one: continuity and procedure are easy to conflate, which is the discrimination the item wants. Dim5 3: the stem presents exactly two needs and asks for exactly two layers, and the key options restate the need vocabulary ('the same way each month', 'computed'), so the mapping is mechanical.

Argued FOR: A — top tier everywhere guarantees no workload is under-served; C — the lightest tier everywhere minimises spend, which is a real mandate; D — a stopwatch trial is empirical rather than dogmatic. Each applies one policy across three different task shapes. Dim3 4 and Dim5 3: with the three tier names supplied, the item resolves to recall of the tier-to-workload mapping rather than applied judgment, and the only option that varies by workload is identifiable without it.

Argued FOR: A — a capability margin above a bar is ordinary risk management; B — side-by-side polish is how teams usually pick; C — the mid tier as professional default is a defensible standing policy. All lose once the stem states both tiers cleared the bar and the office optimises turnaround and cost. ROUND-2 DELTA: the round-1 overlap bounce is discharged — the borrowed vendor clause is gone and the stated constraint survives the rewrite (dim1 5). Dim5 3, down from round 1's 5: the re-expressed stem now names the optimisation target and the cleared bar in the key's own vocabulary (echo screen: 6 vs 3), so the constrained-optimisation answer is handed over. Not a bounce — a pitch cost of the fix, routed to Gate 2.

Argued FOR: B — a lay user may well believe the strongest tier is also the fastest; C — batching is a genuine throughput lever; D — maximum capability as prudence is a real management posture. B inverts the trade-off the evidence already shows, C optimises around the mis-assignment, D is the slogan producing the failure. Dim2 4: B's claim is contradicted inside the stem itself.

Argued FOR: A — silent model swaps are a widely held practitioner belief and would explain the timing; B — forceful phrasing does change output; D — abandoning planning work is a real reaction to a bad week. A is the strong tempter because it fits the observation; it loses because the decline tracks the conversation's growth, not a release. Good-vs-best diagnosis.

Argued FOR: A — waiting for visible degradation avoids paying a transition cost that may never be needed; C — a clean restart is the simplest hygiene; D — long context is designed to hold material. A is the genuine near-miss (act on evidence, not anticipation) and loses because the conclusions become expensive to recover once quality slips. Dim5 5: three remedies, all real, separated only by what must survive.

Argued FOR: A — total recall is what many users assume and would explain the carried preferences; B — rebuilding from documents each session is a defensible discipline; C — restating rules daily does work. A overstates the mechanism, B discards it, C parks a durable rule in the most transient layer. Dim2 4: A's total-recall claim is eliminable without engaging the scenario.

Argued FOR: A — a readable summary is what most people ask for and is genuinely useful; C — designing the process is the outcome the team ultimately wants; D — a narrative that reads complete may well be complete. A drops traceability and testability, C leaps past decisions the stakeholders have not made, D judges by register. Requirements-as-artefact settles it.

Argued FOR: A — consistent, assured output is what practitioners actually use to decide trust; B — peer practice is real evidence of what delegates safely; D — repetitiveness is the standard automation heuristic and is usually right. All three lose to checkability. Dim2 4: D's 'always' converts a good heuristic into a slogan. Dim5 3: all three distractors are surface archetypes (E02/D12/D14), leaving the principled option identifiable without the concept.

Argued FOR: A — an end-stage fact-check is a real and common control; B — remembered utilization is available now and roughly right; C — more spreadsheets genuinely improve estimates. A is the strong near-miss: it checks the same figures the key computes, but only after the plan has been shaped around them. Compute-then-synthesize is a design decision, not a review step.

Argued FOR: B — daily immersion is genuine evidence and the coordinator may well be right; C — automating everything guarantees the real sink is covered; D — a quarterly survey is an existing instrument. B is the honest tempter and loses because vividness is not measurement. Instrumentation before delegation.

Argued FOR: A — the drafts have been strong, so the review hours look like pure overhead; B — one thorough end review is a real and defensible design; D — skipping checkpoints on polished drafts is triage under time pressure. B is the strong contender: it keeps review, just relocates it — and loses because later stages have already built on early-stage errors. Dim5 5.

Argued FOR: A — improving everywhere at once is faster and the proposal has several dimensions; C — hand-writing guarantees the plain-language standard; D — deferring a nearly-right proposal is low-risk. A is the confounded-change error, C discards a strong architecture, D leaves value idle. The review already named the one failing component.

Argued FOR: B — full automation is the efficiency endpoint and the steps are well defined; C — demo impact has real internal-political value; D — keeping the tool out avoids the question entirely. B removes the checkpoint before a quote reaches a customer, C is not a design criterion, D forfeits real gains. Deliberate step selection with the gate intact.

Argued FOR: A — a two-bin sort is simpler to operate and most mappings do collapse to it; B — staff preference is real signal about where the friction is; C — a ready-made classification from a sector conference saves work. A deletes the collaborative middle where most steps belong, B measures comfort rather than risk, C is someone else's mapping. Three criteria, three-way verdict.

Argued FOR: A — catching an error immediately after release is genuinely fast and is how many systems work; C — a timeout keeps the workflow moving and absent approvers are a real operational problem; D — a monthly log review is a real control with an audit trail. A is the strongest: it sounds like a gate and is a report, because the commitment is already made. Dim5 5: position and staffing are the two properties, and each distractor attacks one of them plausibly.

Argued FOR: A — adaptability handles the filings that do not fit the checklist; B — agentic design is genuinely where tooling is heading; D — a pilot demonstration is empirical evidence. A loosens exactly what the process requires fixed, B is a slogan, D is a curated best run. Dim2 4: B argues from trend rather than from the scenario and is discardable on sight.

Argued FOR: B — parallel generation with rubric scoring genuinely does raise draft quality; C — visible rigor has organisational value; D — five drafts gives the duty officer real choice. All three answer requirements nobody stated and add review load or failure modes. Simplest design meeting the stated requirement.

Argued FOR: C — omitting limits genuinely does smooth adoption, and briefings are persuasion documents; D — impressive samples are standard executive communication; E — a full-automation commitment is the ambition executives often want to hear. Each buys a quick yes at the cost of the durable trust the stem asks for. Dim3 4: the item tests general stakeholder-communication judgment more than a Claude-specific competency. Dim5 3: three of five options are transparently self-defeating, so the pair is identifiable without the concept.

Argued FOR: A — the lead is capable and the credentials exist, so building it is the responsive move; C — escalating the whole request is the cautious reading of scope; D — letting it lapse avoids an awkward conversation. C is the genuine near-miss and the reason the item works: over-escalation is as much an error as under-escalation. Dim5 5.

Argued FOR: A — deferring setup to a slack period is ordinary scheduling; B — a peer's failed experiment is real evidence; D — unbillable time is a genuine constraint in a billing firm. Each ignores recurrence, which is the property that makes configuration leverage. The weekly cadence repays the afternoon.

Argued FOR: B — putting everything in instructions is the intuitive fix and instructions are the most obeyed layer; C — a configuration that was set up correctly and does not hold does look defective; D — hand-correction keeps work moving. B swells one mechanism to do three jobs, C misreads mechanism mismatch as a fault, D treats the symptom. Each layer's job settles it; B is a strong near-miss.

Argued FOR: A — a fifth rewrite is what most people do and prompt wording often is the variable; C — more connectors genuinely extend reach; D — an outage would explain repeated failure. A has already failed four times, C hopes a connector exceeds its design, D infers an outage from a scope limit. Dim2 4: D's claim that connectors expose everything the app can do is flatly false and eliminable on sight.

Argued FOR: A — maximum material genuinely improves recall and retrieval is selective anyway; B — internal provenance is a real trust signal; C — a staleness notice is honest and cheap. A maximises unvetted authority, B mistakes origin for currency, C discloses the defect instead of fixing it. Screening plus scoping are the two controls that give the knowledge a warrant.

Argued FOR: A — recency preference is a reasonable assumption about retrieval and often holds; B — deleting the superseded manual is decisive and removes the conflict; C — a merged summary gives one answer. B is the strong near-miss: it works for voucher rules and silently drops everything else the manual still governs. Dim5 5: precedence-by-scope beats three plausible simplifications.

Argued FOR: A — a last-week upload date is the ordinary meaning of 'current' and the teammate's reading is reasonable; B — a monthly cadence does bound staleness; D — a caveat is honest. A is the trap the item is built on, B shrinks an interval that never touched content, D discloses instead of resolving. Dim5 5: metadata-versus-content provenance is a genuine good-vs-best discrimination.

Argued FOR: B — stronger wording is the universal first instinct and sometimes does shift output; C — asking whether the instruction was followed is direct; D — a quarterly overhaul is orderly. B adds intensity to vagueness, C requests an unobservable self-report, D leaves a silent failure standing. Precise and testable is the property at issue.

Argued FOR: A — a cover page genuinely does make rules travel with the files, which sounds like durable placement; B — post-editing removes the offending phrase reliably; C — emphatic restatement is what most people do. A is the sharp near-miss and the item's best distractor: it places the rules inside the very layer that must not carry instruction authority. Dim5 5.

Argued FOR: A — complaints are real signal and no team reviews everything on a schedule; C — a monthly rebuild guarantees nothing ages; D — pasting fresh context each session avoids stale configuration entirely. A is lagging by construction, C scraps working configuration, D trades leverage for daily re-keying. Silent decay is why maintenance must be scheduled.

Argued FOR: A — the output improved and unnecessary announcements do invite debate; B — a standing 'may change' note sets expectations once; D — batching changes into an annual review is orderly governance. All three leave three dependent teams to meet the new structure by surprise. Dim5 3: the three distractors are surface archetypes (D17/D09/D15) and the stem states the dependency outright, so the answer is identifiable without the maintenance-obligation concept.

Argued FOR: A — a blanket exclusion on candidate material is a defensible conservative policy; B — asking the model to apply the written policy is efficient and consistent; C — internal circulation genuinely lowers exposure. A answers before the screen runs, B outsources a judgment that stays with the coordinator, C substitutes readership for consequence. Dim2 4: B is discardable on sight for anyone who knows accountability does not transfer.

Argued FOR: A — the policy does permit AI drafting for exactly this material, so a literal reading authorises sending; C — routing uncovered cases to compliance is cautious and auditable; D — an AI-assistance footer is transparent. A treats silence as permission, C converts practitioner judgment into a queue for every uncovered case, D discloses provenance while leaving an unverified claim about a competitor in the bulletin. Boundaries bound the call; they do not make it.

Argued FOR: A — the upload window is short and pulling data back later is a real remediation path; B — asking the model to check the export is fast; E — a confidentiality instruction is a genuine control on Claude's behaviour. E is the strongest and the reason the item works: it is a control, just one that operates after the records are already inside. Classification precedes movement, and handling follows classification.

Argued FOR: B — if regulated material cannot go to an outside service, abstention is unambiguously compliant and fastest to defend; C — an instruction not to retain is a real vendor-level assurance many teams rely on; D — a confidentiality marking is standard handling. ROUND-2 DELTA: round 1 scored dim1 4 because the borrowed clause left B alive on a strict reading; the rework makes the restriction's object explicit ('regulated identifiers must not leave... though the claim narrative itself carries no such restriction'), which closes B — dim1 now 5, and the overlap bounce is discharged (the vendor clause is gone). Dim5 3, down from round 1's 5: the same sentence that closes B also tells the candidate the narrative is unrestricted, which hands over redact-and-proceed. Not a bounce — the pitch cost of the required fix, routed to Gate 2.

Argued FOR: A — one enterprise agreement is exactly how procurement teams reason about equivalence; B — clearing Memory afterwards is a real control; C — excerpting genuinely reduces exposure volume. A asserts an equivalence the surfaces do not have, B treats retention as cleanup after weeks of exposure, C leaves the same content on the same surface. Dim2 4: A is eliminable on sight for anyone who knows retention differs per surface.

Argued FOR: A — the log is internal and its diagnostic value is real and stated; B — switching logging off is the maximal privacy answer; D — restricting access to two supervisors is a genuine access control. B destroys traceability the team depends on, D leaves indefinite retention of account numbers untouched, A defends convenience against policy. Minimise content, bound retention. Dim5 5: B and D are both real controls aimed at the wrong variable.

Argued FOR: A — the site manager's risk argument may be locally correct and the tender is real; C — asking the model to interpret the policy is quick; D — waiting for the scheduled review respects process. A substitutes personal judgment for the control, C gives a model authority it cannot hold, D lets the tender close unanswered. The exception path exists to be used at speed.

Argued FOR: A — install counts and ratings are the standard trust signal for community software; B — watching the first outputs is empirical and cheap; C — an in-house build removes third-party risk entirely. A measures popularity not permissions, B inspects output not reach, C spends a capability to avoid an afternoon's review. Supply-chain evaluation before enabling.

Argued FOR: B — newer releases are generally better and vendors deprecate old tiers; C — freezing protects regulator-approved assessments from unreviewed change; D — refreshing instructions alongside the tier is efficient. C is the genuine near-miss: it is a real risk posture that fails because the current tier ages against changing material. D confounds two changes. Dim2 4: B argues from release order alone and is discardable on sight.

Argued FOR: A — splitting the paperwork is technically compliant with a literal reading of the block; B — quiet compliance protects a major referral relationship under a real deadline; D — a flat refusal unambiguously holds the line. A defeats the control it appears to satisfy, B leaves the school exposed, D holds the boundary but abandons a partner when a permitted route exists. Dim5 5: D is genuinely defensible and loses only on the 'refusing well' standard.

Argued FOR: A — discomfort is real signal and leaving an uncomfortable use alone is safe; C — another region's approval of the identical use is strong precedent; D — an ethics committee exists precisely for ambiguous cases. A leaves an unrecorded verdict that cannot be reviewed, C transfers a conclusion instead of criteria, D escalates a screen the coordinator can run. Dim5 5: all three are defensible professional instincts.

Argued FOR: A — naming the tool genuinely does invite challenges to sound decisions; B — a signature is a real and traditional accountability mechanism; C — disclosing on request respects those who care without burdening others. B is the strongest and loses because a signature says who is accountable, not how the decision was produced or how to contest it. Dim5 3: the stem's framing ('what does this workflow still owe the student') presupposes an outstanding obligation, which eliminates both 'nothing further' options before the concept is engaged.

Argued FOR: A — a capability upgrade is a plausible response to degraded output; B — a vendor ticket is right if the tool really did change; D — three fixes at once is fastest when a deadline looms. A and B skip four cheap in-team checks, D destroys attribution. The fixed diagnostic order is the competency.

Argued FOR: B — a sampling setting is a real lever on output variability; C — hand-filling two fields is immediate and certain; D — a fix that worked on a similar prompt last month is genuine evidence. C treats the symptom, D borrows a conclusion without naming the layer. Dim2 3: option B is the weak one — temperature is not a control the Associate-scope surfaces expose to a packaging-studio coordinator, so a candidate can discard it without engaging the diagnosis, and it is the only distractor drawn from outside the audience's actual toolkit. Dim6 4 for the same reason: the option puts a knob in the practitioner's hands that their wardrobe does not include. Not a bounce (no dimension ≤2), but it is the weakest distractor in the bank and should be rebuilt from an in-scope layer at the next authoring pass.

Argued FOR: A — three weeks of gains suggest a fourth week would close the gap; B — a stronger model does produce better drafts; C — self-scoring would let the best drafts through untouched. Each keeps tuning a workflow that already performs. Expectation mismatch is the diagnosis, and the stem supplies the promise that was wrong. Dim5 5: the surface invites a tooling fix and the answer is a promise reset.

Argued FOR: A — the combination demonstrably works and shipping what works is pragmatic; C — the model change is the largest lever and a reasonable prior; D — asking the model is quick. A is real but untransferable, C is a prior dressed as a measurement, D asks for a record the model does not hold. Baseline plus one variable.

Argued FOR: A — decomposition often does get legitimate work through; B — the same request worked last quarter, so a product change is a fair hypothesis; D — turning off the configuration is the direct route to the deadline. All three treat the control as the obstacle; the bundle changed, and the permitted portion is what gets done. The Thursday deadline makes each tempting.

Argued FOR: B — asking for higher quality states the complaint plainly; C — three changes at once addresses everything the desk head might have meant; D — wider circulation gathers more actionable critique. B names nothing actionable, C destroys attribution, D collects more feedback before acting on what exists. One named change.

Argued FOR: A — a chat post shares the fix immediately and is searchable; B — schedulers do work things out; C — rebuilding around the working phrasing makes it structural. A preserves text but not the default, B is the status quo that produces the weekly re-derivation, C spends a day on a one-line change. Dim5 5: A is a genuinely reasonable sharing move and loses only on 'by default'.

Argued FOR: B — practitioner perception is real evidence and cheap to collect; C — a faster tier would genuinely enlarge the gain; D — the model can estimate from what it drafted. B is the impression the measurement exists to test, C confounds two changes, D asks for a record the model does not hold. Before and after on the same two figures.

bank_defects_resolution.ccao-f-d3-q34: Round-1 bounce (source-phrase-reuse) RESOLVED — the borrowed 8-word vendor clause is gone from the stem and the quoted-span screen is clean. Dim1 holds at 5. Dim5 falls 5→3: the re-expressed stem states the optimisation target and the cleared quality bar in the key's own vocabulary. Ships; routed to Gate 2 on the 3.
bank_defects_resolution.ccao-f-d6-q65: Round-1 bounce (source-phrase-reuse + dim1 margin) RESOLVED — borrowed clause gone, and making the restriction's object explicit closes option B, lifting dim1 4→5. Dim5 falls 5→3 as a cost of the same sentence. Ships; routed to Gate 2 on the 3.
bank_defects_resolution.process: Round-1 finding F-3 (an Artefact A derivation doc carrying quoted source prose) is NOT an item defect and is not resolved by the rework — it remains open as a ratchet candidate for Gate 2. See overlap-report.md §carried-forward.
